title: Assumed Knowledge
objectives: Relate DNA, genes, alleles and chromosomes.
Use the language of inheritance, populations and evolution precisely.
Distinguish evidence about relatedness from evidence about time.

glossary.definition: A DNA sequence whose information contributes to a functional product, such as an RNA or polypeptide.
An alternative version of a genetic sequence at a locus.
All alleles present in a defined reproducing population.
Observable or measurable characteristics arising from genotype, development and environment.

slides.title: DNA and its building blocks
slides.html: DNA stores genetic information in its base sequence. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, phosphate and one nitrogenous base: adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine. Complementary pairing joins A with T and C with G. The sequence can be copied before cell division, allowing genetic information to pass to daughter cells.

slides.title: Genes occupy loci on chromosomes
slides.html: A chromosome is a long DNA molecule associated with proteins. A gene occupies a particular region, or locus, along that molecule. Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding loci but need not carry identical alleles. Thus a gene describes a functional genetic region, while an allele identifies a particular version of its sequence.

diagram.caption: Letters mark schematic loci; B and b represent alleles at the same locus on homologous chromosomes. They are not individual DNA bases.

slides.title: Chromosome sets and karyotypes
slides.html: Most human nucleated body cells contain 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and a pair of sex chromosomes. Gametes ordinarily contain 23. A karyotype arranges chromosomes for comparison of number and large structural features. Trisomy means an additional copy of one chromosome; polyploidy means additional complete chromosome sets. These terms describe different scales of change.

slides.title: From genotype to phenotype
slides.html: Genotype describes genetic constitution, either at a particular locus or more broadly. Phenotype includes measurable structures, functions and behaviours. It depends on genetic information, which genes are expressed, developmental processes and environmental conditions. A genotype therefore does not always determine one unchanging visible outcome, and different genotypes can sometimes produce similar phenotypes.

diagram.caption: A simplified causal pathway. Environment and development can influence several stages; not every gene codes for a protein.

slides.title: Genomes, populations and alleles
slides.html: A genome includes an organism’s complete genetic material, including non-coding regions. A population must be defined before its gene pool is studied. Allele frequency counts copies of an allele relative to all copies at that locus, rather than simply counting people with a trait. Mutation can introduce new variants; reproduction rearranges inherited combinations.

slides.title: Natural selection and evolution
slides.html: Natural selection occurs when heritable differences are associated with different reproductive success in an environment. Population allele frequencies can then change across generations. Evolution is not an individual deliberately changing its inherited genotype during life. Selection is one evolutionary mechanism; random genetic drift and gene flow can also alter allele frequencies.

slides.title: Classification and common ancestry
slides.html: Classification groups organisms by relationships and shared characteristics. Humans belong to the order Primates and are named Homo sapiens using a genus followed by a specific epithet. Comparative genomics examines genomes for similarities and differences. Shared derived features can help infer common ancestry, but a single resemblance does not by itself establish the whole evolutionary history.

slides.title: Fossils and biological time
slides.html: Fossils preserve remains, impressions or other traces of past life. In an undisturbed sedimentary sequence, lower layers were generally deposited before upper layers: the principle of superposition. Relative dating establishes an order; numerical dating estimates an age or range. An index fossil can help correlate suitable layers but does not automatically date every fossil precisely.

diagram.caption: An invented, undisturbed sedimentary sequence illustrates relative order only. No numerical ages are implied.

slides.title: Interpreting human evolutionary evidence
slides.html: Human evolution is investigated using fossils, anatomy, archaeology and genetic evidence. Braincase shape, teeth and locomotor features can contribute different information. Brain size alone is not a direct measure of intelligence or a complete basis for classifying a fossil. Incomplete samples require conclusions to be qualified and revised when additional evidence becomes available.

slides.title: Biotechnology and evidence
slides.html: Biotechnology uses organisms, cells or biological molecules for particular purposes. DNA analysis can help investigate inheritance, identity and evolutionary relationships. A sound biological explanation separates an observation from its interpretation, states the relevant mechanism and recognises uncertainty. These habits are needed throughout Unit 4, especially when comparing diagrams, measurements and models.

Three copies of chromosome 21 with the other autosomes paired.

options: A was deposited before B in this sequence.
A is exactly twice as old as B.
A must be an ancestor of B.
A and B must belong to the same species.

questions.prompt: Which observation describes evolution at a population level?
options: A person becomes fitter after training.
A child learns a new skill.
An adult temporarily changes gene expression during exercise.
An inherited allele changes in frequency across generations.
feedback: Training is an individual physiological change, not evidence of changing inherited allele frequency.
Learning changes behaviour without necessarily changing a population gene pool.

Correct. Change in allele frequency over generations is a population-genetic description of evolution.
questions.explanation: Correct. Change in allele frequency over generations is a population-genetic description of evolution.

questions.prompt: Explain why two individuals can share the same allele at one locus but show differences in phenotype.
questions.model: An allele at one locus is only part of an individual’s genetic constitution. Other genes, regulatory differences, developmental conditions and environment can influence the measured trait. Even similar genotypes may therefore produce different outcomes. A useful explanation identifies the particular phenotype and a plausible mechanism instead of assuming that one allele completely determines every aspect of the individual.
criteria: Identify the contribution of other genes or regulation.
Explain an environmental or developmental contribution.
Avoid treating one locus as the complete genotype.

questions.prompt: Compare relative dating with numerical dating, and state one limit of inferring evolution from a fossil’s position in a layer.
questions.model: Relative dating places events or specimens in an order, such as lower deposits preceding upper deposits in an undisturbed sequence. Numerical dating estimates an age or age range using additional evidence and assumptions. An older fossil is not automatically the direct ancestor of a younger fossil: they may represent different branches. Disturbance, reworking and incomplete sampling also need consideration.
criteria: Distinguish ordering from estimated age.
State the undisturbed-layer assumption.
Explain why older does not necessarily mean direct ancestor.

summary: Genes are regions of DNA; alleles are alternative versions at a locus.
Phenotype depends on genetic, regulatory, developmental and environmental influences.
Allele frequencies describe a defined population’s gene pool.
Fossils, anatomical comparisons and genomes provide different kinds of evolutionary evidence.

slides.title: Changes in genetic material
slides.html: Differences in genetic information contribute to variation between individuals. One source of these differences is mutation: a lasting change in genetic material.

slides.title: Changes in genetic material
slides.html:
What is a mutation?

A mutation may change a DNA base sequence. Larger genetic changes can alter chromosome structure or chromosome number. The effect depends on which genetic material changes, where the change occurs and how it affects cell function.

slides.title: Changes in genetic material
slides.html: A mutagen is an agent that increases the frequency of mutations. An allele is an alternative version of a gene.

slides.title: Changes in genetic material
slides.html: These effects are context-dependent. A variant that is useful in one environment may be disadvantageous in another. A mutation also need not produce an obvious visible change.

slides.title: Changes in genetic material
slides.html: Key idea: mutations do not arise because an organism needs a particular change. Their consequences are not directed towards solving the organism’s problems.

slides.title: How mutations arise
slides.html: Mutations may arise spontaneously or be induced by mutagens. A spontaneous mutation can occur when DNA is copied incorrectly and the error is not repaired. Errors during cell division can also alter chromosome distribution.

slides.title: How mutations arise
slides.html:
Mutagens

Some environmental agents damage DNA or interfere with its copying. Exposure can increase mutation frequency, although it does not ensure that a particular mutation will occur.

slides.html:
Can the change be passed to offspring?

This depends on the affected cell. Somatic cells are body cells outside the cell lineage that produces gametes. A mutation in a somatic cell can be copied into its daughter cells, but is not normally passed to offspring through sexual reproduction.

slides.title: How mutations arise
slides.html: A germline mutation occurs in a gamete or in a cell that gives rise to gametes. It may be inherited if a gamete carrying that change contributes to fertilisation.

Example · Two different cell types

A mutation in a skin cell may spread within that person as the cell divides. A mutation in an egg cell may be present in the resulting offspring if that egg is fertilised.

Reasoning: inheritance depends on whether the altered genetic material enters the offspring through a gamete.

slides.title: How mutations arise
slides.html: Be precise: being located in an ovary or testis does not automatically make a cell a germline cell. The important issue is whether it belongs to the gamete-producing lineage.

slides.title: Changes to a base sequence
slides.html: A gene-level mutation alters a DNA sequence. A base substitution, often described as a point mutation, replaces one base with another. An insertion adds bases, while a deletion removes them.

slides.title: Changes to a base sequence
slides.html:
From DNA to protein

For a protein-coding gene, information in DNA is transcribed into mRNA. During translation, the ribosome reads mRNA in groups of three bases called codons. A codon specifies an amino acid or a stop signal.

slides.html: DNA sequence→mRNA codons→Amino acid sequence→Protein structure and function

slides.title: Changes to a base sequence
slides.html: A base change may leave the amino acid unchanged, replace an amino acid, or introduce a stop signal. Its effect on the protein is therefore not always the same.

Insertions, deletions and the reading frame

Adding or removing a number of bases that is not a multiple of three within a coding region changes how downstream bases are grouped. This is a frameshift. It can alter many later amino acids and may introduce an early stop codon.

A single-base substitution changes one triplet. Later groups stay in the same reading frame. This particular example would produce an mRNA stop codon (UAA).

slides.title: Changes to a base sequence
slides.html: Important distinction: a substitution does not shift the reading frame. An insertion or deletion of three bases also preserves the downstream grouping, although the protein sequence can still change.

slides.title: Changes on a larger scale
slides.html: Chromosome-level changes affect chromosome structure or number. They can involve many genes at once, so their consequences may be broader than those of a single-base change.

slides.html: A karyotype displays chromosomes arranged into groups or pairs. It can reveal chromosome-number changes and sufficiently large structural changes. An ordinary karyotype cannot show a single-base substitution.

slides.html: Keep the scale clear: a missing DNA base within a gene and a missing chromosome segment are both deletions, but they occur at different scales.

slides.title: New alleles and natural selection
slides.html: Mutation supplies new genetic variants. When a mutation changes a gene, it can produce a new allele. If that change is inherited, it may contribute to variation in a population.

slides.title: New alleles and natural selection
slides.html:
New alleles versus new combinations

Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation usually produce new combinations of existing alleles. Mutation is the original source of new alleles. These processes contribute to genetic variation in different ways.

slides.title: New alleles and natural selection
slides.html:
Selection acts on existing variation

Individuals with an inherited variant that improves reproductive success in a particular environment may contribute more offspring to the next generation. Over generations, the associated allele may become more common.

slides.title: New alleles and natural selection
slides.html:
Explained example · A changing environment

A population already contains individuals with a heritable variant that helps them tolerate a new environmental condition. Those individuals survive and reproduce more successfully. Their descendants inherit the variant, so its frequency can increase.

Cause-and-effect chain: inherited variation → different reproductive success → a change in allele frequency over generations.

slides.html: Harmful alleles are not necessarily removed immediately. For example, a recessive allele can be carried by a heterozygous individual without producing the recessive phenotype. New mutations can also introduce harmful alleles again.

slides.title: New alleles and natural selection
slides.html: Avoid this explanation: “The organism mutated because it needed to survive.” Mutation does not anticipate a need; selection changes the frequency of inherited variants.

title: Mutation and Polypeptide Synthesis
objectives: Trace a coding-sequence change through transcription and translation.
Distinguish synonymous, missense and nonsense outcomes.
Explain why protein effects depend on position and cell lineage.

glossary.definition: A three-base mRNA sequence specifying an amino acid or translation stop signal.
A substitution that changes the amino acid specified by a codon.
A substitution that creates a premature stop codon.
A substitution that leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged.

slides.title: Information is read in stages
slides.html: A protein-coding DNA sequence is transcribed into RNA. After appropriate processing in a human cell, the mRNA is translated by a ribosome. The ribosome reads codons in a defined frame, and tRNAs deliver the corresponding amino acids. A change in DNA can therefore influence the amino acid sequence, but its effect must be traced rather than assumed.

diagram.caption: This simplified pathway applies to protein-coding genes. Regulatory mutations can affect the amount of product rather than its amino acid sequence.

slides.title: Identify the strand and direction
slides.html: A codon table is read using mRNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction. The coding DNA strand has the same sequence as that mRNA, except that DNA contains T where RNA contains U. The template strand is complementary and antiparallel to the RNA. An unlabelled DNA triplet cannot be interpreted reliably without knowing which strand and direction are shown.

slides.title: A synonymous change
slides.html: The genetic code is degenerate: more than one codon can specify the same amino acid. For example, mRNA GAA and GAG both specify glutamate. A substitution between these codons is synonymous because the amino acid is unchanged. Synonymous does not mean every possible molecular effect is absent, but it does identify the unchanged amino acid in this comparison.

diagram.caption: Coding DNA is shown 5′ to 3′. GAA becomes GAG, so the corresponding mRNA codons both encode glutamate; downstream grouping is unchanged.

slides.title: A missense change
slides.html: Changing coding DNA GAA to GTA changes the corresponding mRNA codon from GAA to GUA. The codon now specifies valine instead of glutamate. This is a missense substitution. Whether the replacement seriously changes function depends on the amino acids, their position, the protein’s structure and the biological role of the affected region.

slides.title: A nonsense change
slides.html: If coding DNA GAA changes to TAA, the corresponding mRNA changes from GAA to UAA. UAA is a stop codon rather than an amino-acid codon. An early stop can produce a shortened polypeptide or cause the RNA to be degraded. The extent of the effect depends partly on where the premature stop occurs and how the cell processes that RNA.

slides.title: Protein structure links sequence to function
slides.html: A polypeptide’s amino acid sequence influences interactions involved in folding and binding. A change at an enzyme’s active site can affect substrate binding or catalysis. A change in a less critical region may have little detectable effect. Consequently, neither a changed amino acid nor a shorter chain is enough on its own to quantify the impact on the organism.

slides.title: Location within the organism matters
slides.html: A mutation arising in a body-cell lineage can affect that cell and its descendants. A mutation in a gamete-producing lineage may enter a gamete and be inherited if that gamete contributes at fertilisation. Germline origin does not guarantee transmission to every child. A mutation occurring after fertilisation may produce mosaicism, with only some cell lineages carrying it.

slides.title: Explaining a biological consequence
slides.html: A complete explanation links sequence, RNA, polypeptide and cell function. For example, reduced production of a required enzyme may lower the rate of a particular reaction and alter a cell’s behaviour. Do not skip directly from “DNA changed” to a named disease without evidence. Different variants in the same gene can have different consequences, and many mutations have no obvious phenotype.

options: The protein must be completely inactive.

questions.prompt: Trace the effect of changing coding DNA GAA to GTA on a polypeptide, using the facts that GAA encodes glutamate and GUA encodes valine in mRNA.
questions.model: The coding DNA sequence is transcribed into an mRNA sequence that matches it except for U replacing T. The mRNA codon therefore changes from GAA to GUA. During translation, valine is inserted at that position instead of glutamate. The replacement may alter folding or interactions and hence protein function, but its actual effect depends on the protein and the location of the substitution.
criteria: Correctly derive GUA from coding DNA GTA.
Identify glutamate being replaced by valine.
Qualify the possible functional effect.

questions.prompt: Explain why an early nonsense substitution can have a more extensive effect than a synonymous substitution, without claiming that every nonsense variant has the same severity.
questions.model: A synonymous substitution leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged in the comparison. A nonsense substitution introduces a stop codon, potentially ending translation before the normal end or triggering RNA degradation. It may therefore remove an important protein region or reduce protein production. Severity still depends on position, RNA processing, the gene’s function and whether other functional copies or products compensate.
criteria: Distinguish amino-acid preservation from a premature stop.
Link the stop to shortened or reduced protein production.
State a reason severity varies.

summary: Read codon tables using mRNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
Synonymous, missense and nonsense describe different consequences of substitutions.
Sequence changes must be linked mechanistically to protein and cell function.
Inheritance depends on the affected lineage and contribution to offspring.

title: Point Mutations
objectives: Classify substitutions and small insertions or deletions.
Explain synonymous, missense, nonsense and frameshift outcomes.
Use labelled sequences to justify a predicted effect.

glossary.definition: In the narrow usage here, a change affecting a single nucleotide position.
The grouping of a coding sequence into successive triplets for translation.
A change in downstream triplet grouping caused by a coding-region insertion or deletion not divisible by three.
An insertion or deletion preserving the downstream reading frame, commonly because its length is divisible by three.

slides.title: Define the scale before naming the effect
slides.html: A gene mutation changes a DNA sequence within or associated with a gene. In a narrow and common usage, a point mutation affects one nucleotide position, especially a base substitution. Small insertions and deletions are also gene-level changes. Naming the event and then describing its consequence is more precise than using “point mutation” for every small rearrangement.

slides.title: Base substitution preserves sequence length
slides.html: A substitution replaces one base pair with another without changing the number of base pairs. In a coding region, the altered triplet may specify the same amino acid, a different amino acid or a stop signal. These are synonymous, missense and nonsense outcomes respectively. The substitution itself does not shift the downstream reading frame.

diagram.caption: Coding DNA is shown 5′ to 3′. Replacing the second base of GAA produces GTA; the total sequence length and downstream triplet grouping remain unchanged.

slides.title: Degeneracy explains synonymous substitutions
slides.html: Different mRNA codons can specify the same amino acid. For example, GUU and GUG both specify valine. A substitution between them is synonymous at the amino-acid level. By contrast, changing GAA to GUA replaces glutamate with valine. The codon table identifies the sequence consequence; experimental or other evidence is needed to establish the full functional effect.

slides.title: Missense and nonsense have different meanings
slides.html: A missense substitution changes an encoded amino acid. A nonsense substitution creates a stop codon where an amino acid would normally be specified. UAA, UAG and UGA are the standard mRNA stop codons. The effect of a premature stop depends on its position and RNA processing; “nonsense” is not simply a synonym for any harmful mutation.

slides.title: An insertion can shift the frame
slides.html: An insertion adds one or more nucleotides. If one base is inserted within a coding sequence, bases after the insertion are regrouped into different triplets. The affected codon and later codons may change, potentially producing an early stop. The upstream sequence remains unchanged, so the position of the insertion matters when explaining how much of the polypeptide is affected.

diagram.caption: Coding DNA, 5′ to 3′. Inserting C after ATG changes grouping from ATG|GAA|CCT|TGC to ATG|CGA|ACC|TTG|C. The last base is only an incomplete excerpt, not a codon.

slides.title: Deletion and the three-base exception
slides.html: Deleting one or two bases within a coding region shifts the downstream frame. Deleting three bases preserves the grouping of later codons, although it can remove an amino acid and alter codons around the deletion boundary. Preserving the frame does not guarantee a harmless outcome: a removed residue may be important for folding, binding or catalysis.

slides.title: Position and lineage influence consequences
slides.html: A small change near the beginning of a coding sequence can affect more downstream translation than a similar event near the end. However, severity cannot be ranked from position alone. Regulatory location, protein function and the affected cell lineage also matter. A somatic variant can affect a tissue without being inherited through gametes; a germline variant may be transmitted.

slides.title: Write a justified sequence explanation
slides.html: First identify whether bases were replaced, added or removed. State the strand and direction, derive the relevant mRNA and group it into codons. Compare the encoded products and then explain a plausible functional effect with appropriate qualification. For a longer reversed segment, use the term inversion and specify its length rather than assuming that every inversion is a one-base event.

questions.prompt: A base substitution changes one mRNA codon from GUU to GUG; both encode valine. What is the immediate coding consequence?
options: A frameshift
A premature stop
A duplicated chromosome
A synonymous substitution
feedback: The number of bases has not changed, so the frame is preserved.
Neither of these codons is a stop codon.
A single codon comparison gives no evidence of chromosome duplication.
Correct. The codon changes while the encoded amino acid remains valine.
questions.explanation: Correct. The codon changes while the encoded amino acid remains valine.

questions.prompt: Which coding-region change must preserve the downstream reading frame, although it may still affect function?
options: Deletion of one base
Insertion of two bases
Deletion of three consecutive bases
Deletion of five consecutive bases
feedback: A one-base deletion changes downstream triplet grouping.
Two added bases are not a multiple of three.
Correct. Three bases preserve the downstream frame; the local amino-acid sequence can still change.
Five bases are not a multiple of three.
questions.explanation: Correct. Three bases preserve the downstream frame; the local amino-acid sequence can still change.

questions.prompt: Which term specifically describes a substitution that creates UAG within the translated region?
options: Nonsense
Synonymous
Reciprocal translocation
Polyploidy
feedback: Correct. UAG is an mRNA stop codon, so a premature UAG is a nonsense outcome.
Synonymous means the amino acid is unchanged, not replaced by a stop.
Translocation moves chromosome segments between locations.
Polyploidy changes complete chromosome sets.
questions.explanation: Correct. UAG is an mRNA stop codon, so a premature UAG is a nonsense outcome.

questions.prompt: A coding sequence changes from ATG|GAA|CCT|TGC to ATG|CGA|ACC|TTG|C. What best explains this comparison?
options: One base substitution after the start codon
A one-base insertion after ATG
Three bases deleted from the end
A chromosome-wide inversion
feedback: A substitution preserves sequence length and downstream grouping.
Correct. Adding C after ATG shifts all complete downstream triplets.
The changed sequence contains an additional base rather than three fewer bases.
This comparison shows a local added base, not reversed chromosome order.
questions.explanation: Correct. Adding C after ATG shifts all complete downstream triplets.

questions.prompt: Explain why deleting one base and deleting three bases from a coding region can have different downstream consequences.
questions.model: A ribosome reads mRNA in groups of three bases. Removing one base changes how later bases are grouped, so many downstream codons can differ and an early stop may appear. Removing three bases preserves the downstream frame, although it can remove an amino acid or alter the local sequence at the boundary. Neither event’s severity can be established from its size alone.
criteria: Explain triplet grouping.
Contrast frameshift with downstream frame preservation.
Recognise that an in-frame deletion may still affect function.

questions.prompt: A student says, “A missense mutation is always more harmful than a synonymous mutation.” Evaluate this statement.
questions.model: Missense identifies a changed amino acid, while synonymous identifies no amino-acid change in the comparison. These terms do not provide a universal ranking of harm. A missense replacement may have little effect if the residue is non-critical or chemically similar. Synonymous changes may sometimes influence RNA processing or expression. The relevant location, gene function and evidence must be considered before judging the phenotype.
criteria: Define both outcomes correctly.
Reject an automatic severity ranking.
Identify evidence or context needed to assess function.

summary: Separate the DNA event from its RNA and protein consequences.
Substitutions preserve reading frame but can have different coding outcomes.
Coding-region indels not divisible by three can cause frameshifts.
Neither a mutation label nor its location alone proves its phenotypic severity.
sourceNotes: Scope follows Chapter 4, printed pages 5–6.
Terminology clarified: point mutation is used narrowly; small indels are named explicitly and inversions are described by their extent.
Corrected “silent” usage: synonymous means unchanged amino acid, not merely a similar replacement. Three-base indels preserve downstream frame but are not necessarily harmless.

title: Block Mutations
objectives: Identify deletion, duplication, inversion and translocation of chromosome segments.
Explain how rearrangements affect gene dosage, gene integrity or regulation.
Relate repeats and duplicated genes to genomic variation.

glossary.definition: A structural change involving a segment of a chromosome.
The number of copies of a gene or genetic region and its potential influence on product amount.
Adjacent copies of a repeated DNA sequence.
An exchange of segments between non-homologous chromosomes.

slides.title: Structural change at chromosome scale
slides.html: A block mutation changes a segment of a chromosome rather than a single base alone. It may remove, copy, reverse or relocate genetic material. Some changes affect many loci; others disrupt a single important gene at a breakpoint. Consequences depend on what material is involved and whether gene dosage, sequence integrity or regulation changes.

slides.title: Deletion removes genetic material
slides.html: A deletion removes a chromosome segment. Any genes or regulatory sequences within that region may be lost from that chromosome. A large deletion can affect several functions, but a small deletion at a critical location can also have a major effect. Cri du chat syndrome is associated with a deletion involving the short arm of chromosome 5; deletion extent can vary.

diagram.caption: Letters mark chromosome segments. C has been lost; they do not represent single nucleotide bases.

slides.title: Duplication changes copy number
slides.html: A duplication produces an additional copy of a DNA region. It may alter the dosage of genes in that region or create adjacent repeated sequences. Unequal crossing over is one mechanism that can produce a duplication in one product and a corresponding deletion in another. An extra copy is not automatically advantageous: expression balance and the affected genes matter.

diagram.caption: A schematic duplication of segment C. The letters show order and copy number, not the relative physical lengths of the regions.

slides.title: Inversion reverses orientation
slides.html: An inversion occurs when a segment is reinserted in reverse orientation. Total DNA amount can remain unchanged, but a breakpoint can disrupt a gene or change its regulatory context. In a heterozygous carrier, pairing and recombination within the inverted region can complicate the production of balanced gametes. A normal-looking carrier therefore does not prove that every reproductive outcome is unaffected.

slides.title: Translocation changes chromosome location
slides.html: A translocation relocates material, often between non-homologous chromosomes. In a reciprocal translocation, two chromosomes exchange segments. A balanced rearrangement may preserve the total amount of material but can still interrupt a gene or alter regulation. Rearranged chromosomes can also produce unbalanced gametes, so a carrier’s phenotype and reproductive outcomes require separate consideration.

diagram.caption: An original schematic reciprocal exchange of end segments D and O. The chromosomes are non-homologous, unlike a normal exchange between homologous chromatids.

slides.title: Repeats and genetic markers
slides.html: Tandem repeats contain adjacent copies of a sequence motif. Repeat number can vary among individuals, creating alleles useful as genetic markers. Short tandem repeats are used in DNA profiling, where multiple loci are compared. A matching marker pattern is evidence that must be evaluated with population frequencies, sample quality and other information rather than treated as a direct reading of every trait.

slides.title: Repeat expansion can affect function
slides.html: Some genes contain short repeated motifs whose copy number can expand. In certain disorders, a repeat expansion affects the gene product or gene regulation. For example, expanded CAG repeats in HTT are associated with Huntington disease. Disease interpretation depends on the particular locus and repeat range; a statement that all repeated DNA is harmful is incorrect.

slides.title: Duplicated genes and long-term evolution
slides.html: If an entire gene is duplicated and both copies are inherited, later mutations can make the copies diverge. One may retain an ancestral function while the other changes in regulation or function, although many duplicates are lost or disabled. Related genes can form a gene family. Similar sequence and function within a family can therefore reflect shared origin through duplication.

diagram.caption: A possible evolutionary outcome, not an inevitable fate of every duplication. Some copies are lost or become non-functional.

slides.title: Mutation hotspots and interpretation
slides.html: Mutation frequency is not identical across all DNA positions. Repeated or chemically susceptible sequences can make particular regions more prone to certain changes. A hotspot describes a higher observed mutation rate, not a useful change directed by the organism. When interpreting a rearrangement diagram, identify the original order, locate the changed region and state the evidence for the particular category.

questions.prompt: A chromosome order A–B–C–D–E changes to A–B–C–C–D–E. Which event is shown?
options: Inversion
Duplication
Deletion
Trisomy
feedback: An inversion reverses orientation; this diagram instead shows an added copy of C.
Correct. Segment C appears twice.
A deletion removes material rather than copying C.
Trisomy adds a whole copy of a chromosome, not just the depicted segment.
questions.explanation: Correct. Segment C appears twice.

questions.prompt: Two non-homologous chromosomes exchange end segments. What is the most specific description?
options: Independent assortment
Synonymous substitution
Reciprocal translocation
Normal segregation
feedback: Independent assortment concerns combinations of homologues in gametes.
A synonymous substitution concerns a codon’s amino-acid outcome.
Correct. Reciprocal translocation exchanges material between non-homologous chromosomes.
Segregation separates chromosomes; it does not exchange their end segments.
questions.explanation: Correct. Reciprocal translocation exchanges material between non-homologous chromosomes.

questions.prompt: Why can a balanced inversion still matter biologically?
options: Every inversion adds a complete chromosome set.
It necessarily removes every gene in the segment.
It always prevents DNA replication.
Breakpoints can disrupt genes or alter regulation even without net DNA loss.
feedback: An inversion reverses a segment; it does not inherently add whole sets.
The segment may be retained, but in reverse orientation.
Replication failure is not an inevitable consequence.
Correct. Preserved amount does not guarantee preserved gene function or reproductive outcomes.
questions.explanation: Correct. Preserved amount does not guarantee preserved gene function or reproductive outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains the usefulness of short tandem repeats in DNA profiling?
options: Individuals may carry different repeat-number alleles at the same locus.
All individuals have exactly the same repeat number.
Each repeat gives a complete account of a person’s phenotype.
Repeat variation can only arise by adding whole chromosomes.
feedback: Correct. Variable repeat numbers provide informative marker differences, especially across multiple loci.
If repeat counts were identical in everyone, that marker would not distinguish samples.
A marker is not a complete prediction of phenotype.
Repeat-number changes can occur within a chromosome without changing whole-chromosome count.
questions.explanation: Correct. Variable repeat numbers provide informative marker differences, especially across multiple loci.

questions.prompt: Compare deletion and inversion, explaining why both can affect phenotype even though only one necessarily removes the depicted segment.
questions.model: A deletion removes a chromosome segment and may reduce the dosage of genes or regulatory elements in that region. An inversion retains a segment but reverses its orientation, so total DNA amount can be preserved. Nevertheless, inversion breakpoints can disrupt genes or change regulatory relationships. Their consequences depend on the affected location, and rearrangements can also influence the balanced chromosome combinations produced during meiosis.
criteria: Distinguish removal from reversed orientation.
Link deletion to loss or dosage.
Explain a possible inversion effect without assuming DNA loss.

questions.prompt: Explain how gene duplication can contribute to a gene family, and give one reason duplication is not automatically beneficial.
questions.model: Duplication provides an additional copy of a gene. If both copies are inherited, mutations can accumulate separately, producing related sequences with differences in regulation or function. Retained descendants may form a gene family with evidence of shared origin. Duplication can also upset expression balance or increase a harmful dosage, and many copies are eventually lost or disabled. A beneficial new function is therefore only one possible outcome.
criteria: Link duplication to inherited additional copies.
Explain divergence and shared origin.
State a possible cost or loss of duplicate copies.

summary: Block mutations alter chromosome segments and may change dosage, orientation or location.
Balanced rearrangements are not automatically harmless.
Repeat-number variation can provide genetic markers or, at particular loci, affect function.
Inherited duplication and divergence can contribute to gene families.
sourceNotes: Scope follows Chapter 5, printed pages 7–8.
Clinical details are illustrative rather than diagnostic; exact penetrance thresholds and categorical infertility claims are not taught.
Balanced rearrangements are distinguished from normal homologous crossing over; gene disruption and reproductive effects are qualified.

title: Transposable Genetic Elements
objectives: Compare DNA transposons with retrotransposons.
Explain insertional and regulatory effects of transposition.
Distinguish movement within a genome from movement between organisms.

glossary.definition: A DNA sequence with the ability, currently or historically, to change genomic position through transposition.
Movement or copying of a transposable element into another genomic location.
An enzyme that catalyses steps in the movement of many DNA transposons.
A transposable element that uses an RNA intermediate and reverse transcription.

slides.title: Mobile sequences in genomes
slides.html: Transposable elements are DNA sequences that can change location or produce copies at new genomic locations. They occur in many groups of organisms. “Jumping gene” is an informal name, not a literal description of physical jumping and not a guarantee that every element encodes a functional gene. Many inherited element-derived sequences are no longer capable of autonomous movement.

slides.title: A DNA cut-and-paste model
slides.html: In a simplified DNA transposon mechanism, transposase recognises element ends and helps remove the DNA element from its original site. The element is inserted at another location and the DNA is repaired. Movement can interrupt a functional sequence at the destination; imperfect repair at the original site can also leave a change. Mechanisms differ among element families.

diagram.caption: T marks a whole transposable DNA element, not thymine. The model illustrates one cut-and-paste event at different genomic loci.

slides.title: Retrotransposons use an RNA intermediate
slides.html: A retrotransposon is transcribed into RNA. Reverse transcription produces a DNA copy that can integrate elsewhere. The source copy can remain, so this is commonly described as copy-and-paste transposition. Some elements supply their own movement machinery while others depend on proteins made by other elements. Retrotransposition is not simply RNA being cut out and pasted directly into DNA.

diagram.caption: A simplified copy-and-paste retrotransposition pathway. The original DNA copy can remain at its locus.

slides.title: An insertion may disrupt a gene
slides.html: An element inserted into a coding sequence can alter the reading frame, interrupt normal RNA processing or introduce signals that change transcription. The consequence depends on its position and orientation. Insertion into an essential functional region may impair a product, while insertion elsewhere may have little detectable effect. Not every new insertion produces a disease or visible phenotype.

slides.title: Regulation can change without destroying a gene
slides.html: Elements can carry promoters, enhancers or other regulatory sequences. Insertion near a gene may alter where, when or how much that gene is expressed. Over long evolutionary periods, some element-derived sequences have acquired useful host functions. It is therefore misleading to label every element “junk”, even though many copies make no currently recognised useful product.

slides.title: Repeated sequences and rearrangements
slides.html: Similar element copies at different genomic positions can provide sites for misaligned recombination. Depending on their arrangement, recombination can delete, duplicate or invert intervening DNA. This links mobile elements with larger structural changes, but transposition and recombination are distinct processes. A rearrangement should be explained from the particular sequence organisation rather than attributed automatically to any repeat.

slides.title: Movement within and between cells
slides.html: In bacteria, a transposable element can move between a chromosome and a plasmid and may carry an antibiotic-resistance gene. Transfer of that plasmid between bacteria is a separate mechanism of horizontal gene transfer. Transposition changes an element’s genomic location; cell-to-cell transfer allows genetic material to enter another organism. The processes can work together without being identical.

slides.title: Inheritance and historical evidence
slides.html: A new insertion in a human somatic lineage may affect only that person’s affected cells. An insertion in a gamete-producing lineage may be inherited if it enters an offspring. Barbara McClintock’s maize research helped establish mobile genetic elements as a real mechanism of genome change. Their evolutionary importance includes mutational effects, regulatory changes and the accumulation of repeated sequences.

questions.prompt: Which pathway characterises a retrotransposon?
options: DNA element removed and its RNA pasted directly into a chromosome.
RNA transcript, reverse transcription to DNA, then integration of a DNA copy.
A protein physically changing into a chromosome.
Movement of an entire organism between populations.
feedback: RNA is not simply pasted into chromosomal DNA in the retrotransposition mechanism.
Correct. Retrotransposition uses an RNA intermediate and a new DNA copy.
Proteins do not become chromosomes by transposition.
Organism migration is not transposition within a genome.
questions.explanation: Correct. Retrotransposition uses an RNA intermediate and a new DNA copy.

questions.prompt: In the chromosome diagram, T moves from A–T–B–C to L–T–M–N. T represents an entire mobile element. Which description fits?
options: Trisomy of chromosome T
A synonymous codon change
Cut-and-paste transposition in the simplified model
Independent assortment of allele T
feedback: The label denotes an element, not an extra chromosome.
The diagram does not compare codons or amino acids.
Correct. The element leaves one locus and enters another.
Independent assortment concerns chromosome combinations, not relocation of this element.
questions.explanation: Correct. The element leaves one locus and enters another.

questions.prompt: Why can an insertion near a promoter affect phenotype even if the coding sequence remains intact?
options: It must always remove the coding region.
Promoters never influence RNA production.
Only chromosome-number changes can alter expression.
It can alter when or how much a gene is transcribed.
feedback: An insertion can affect regulation without deleting coding DNA.
Promoters participate in transcription initiation and regulation.
Sequence changes near genes can alter expression without changing chromosome number.
Correct. Regulatory context can change gene product amounts or locations.
questions.explanation: Correct. Regulatory context can change gene product amounts or locations.

questions.prompt: A resistance-bearing transposon enters a plasmid, and that plasmid transfers to another bacterium. Which statement is correct?
options: Transposition and plasmid transfer are different processes that can act together.
Transposition itself is always the whole cell-to-cell transfer process.
Plasmids are amino-acid chains without DNA.
Only mutations in human gametes can change DNA position.
feedback: Correct. Relocation within genetic material and transfer between cells are distinct mechanisms.
Transposition describes element relocation, not every step of transfer between bacteria.
Plasmids are DNA molecules, not polypeptides.
Transposition is not restricted to humans or gametes.
questions.explanation: Correct. Relocation within genetic material and transfer between cells are distinct mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Compare DNA transposon cut-and-paste movement with retrotransposon copy-and-paste movement.
questions.model: In a simplified DNA transposon mechanism, an element is removed as DNA and inserted elsewhere, with repair of the original and target sites. Retrotransposition involves transcription into RNA, reverse transcription into a DNA copy and integration of that copy. The original retrotransposon sequence can remain, potentially increasing copy number. Element families vary, so these descriptions are models rather than universal details of every element.
criteria: Identify DNA relocation in the cut-and-paste model.
Include RNA and reverse transcription for retrotransposition.
Explain why copy number can increase.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways that a transposable-element insertion can affect a gene, and why an insertion does not automatically cause a harmful phenotype.
questions.model: An insertion within a gene can disrupt its coding sequence or normal RNA processing, changing the functional product. An insertion near regulatory DNA can alter transcription and therefore product amount or expression pattern. The outcome depends on insertion position, orientation, affected function and cellular context. Some insertions have little detectable effect, and some element-derived sequences have acquired host functions, so harm cannot be inferred from the label alone.
criteria: Explain a coding or RNA-processing effect.
Explain a regulatory effect.
Qualify consequences using location or context.

summary: Transposable elements can move or copy into new genomic positions.
Retrotransposons use RNA and reverse transcription rather than direct RNA insertion.
Insertions can alter coding sequences, RNA processing or gene regulation.
Transposition within genetic material and transfer between organisms are distinct processes.
sourceNotes: Scope follows Chapter 6, printed page 9.
Corrected the source’s description of retrotransposons as cut-and-paste RNA: the lesson teaches RNA intermediate, reverse transcription and DNA integration.
Avoided unsupported claims that one insertion is the most common form of haemophilia and that all transposable elements lack useful host functions.

title: Chromosome Abnormalities
objectives: Distinguish aneuploidy from changes in complete chromosome sets.
Compare nondisjunction in meiosis I, meiosis II and mitosis.
Interpret chromosome counts without assuming a uniform phenotype.

glossary.definition: An abnormal number of particular chromosomes rather than complete chromosome sets.
More than two complete chromosome sets in a cell.
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate correctly.
The presence of two or more genetically different cell populations derived from one zygote.

slides.title: Count chromosomes and complete sets separately
slides.html: Typical human gametes contain one set of 23 chromosomes, while most nucleated body cells contain two sets. Aneuploidy changes the number of particular chromosomes. Monosomy means one copy rather than the usual two; trisomy means three. Polyploidy changes complete sets, such as three complete sets in triploidy. A missing segment is a structural change, not the same event as losing a whole chromosome.

slides.title: Trisomy changes a particular chromosome count
slides.html: In a typical body cell, chromosome 21 is represented by two homologues. A cell with three separate copies has trisomy 21 and commonly contains 47 chromosomes in total. However, extra chromosome-21 material can also be present through a translocation, so total chromosome count alone does not describe every case. A karyotype must be examined for both number and structure.

diagram.caption: Only copies of chromosome 21 are shown. Three separate copies commonly yield 47 total chromosomes; translocation forms require structural interpretation.

slides.title: Meiosis I nondisjunction
slides.html: During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes normally separate into different daughter cells. If one homologous pair fails to separate, both members enter the same cell. If subsequent divisions occur normally, two resulting gametes contain an extra copy of that chromosome and two lack it. All four products are therefore abnormal for the chromosome pair involved.

nodes: Homologues fail to separate in meiosis I
Two n+1 and two n−1 gametes
diagram.caption: One affected chromosome pair is followed; other chromosomes are assumed to segregate normally.

slides.title: Meiosis II nondisjunction
slides.html: During meiosis II, sister chromatids normally separate. If this fails in one daughter cell after a normal meiosis I, the other daughter cell can still divide normally. The four products then include two normal gametes, one with an extra copy and one lacking that chromosome. This product pattern differs from nondisjunction of homologues in meiosis I.

nodes: Sister chromatids fail to separate in one cell
Two n gametes, one n+1 and one n−1
diagram.caption: This simplified model assumes one meiosis-II nondisjunction event and otherwise normal segregation.

slides.title: Fertilisation changes the zygote count
slides.html: A gamete carrying an extra chromosome may combine with a normal gamete to produce a trisomic zygote. For humans, 24 plus 23 gives 47. A gamete lacking one chromosome may yield a monosomic zygote after fertilisation. Many chromosome imbalances disrupt development, but survival and phenotype depend on the chromosome and genetic material involved rather than the count alone.

slides.title: Mitotic errors can produce mosaicism
slides.html: Nondisjunction during mitosis after fertilisation can generate cell lineages with different chromosome numbers in the same individual. Later divisions copy those differences within descendant lineages. An earlier event may affect more tissues than a later event, but cell survival and developmental contribution also matter. Mosaicism describes this mixture of cell populations, not two separate fertilisation events.

slides.title: Sex-chromosome examples require qualification
slides.html: Examples of sex-chromosome aneuploidy include 47,XXY, 45,X, 47,XYY and 47,XXX. They can have varied effects, and mosaic forms also occur. X-chromosome inactivation reduces expression from much of extra X chromosomes, but some genes escape inactivation. It is therefore incorrect to claim that extra X chromosomes have no consequences or that every affected individual has identical traits or fertility.

slides.title: Structure can change without changing the total
slides.html: Unequal crossing over can generate a duplicated region in one chromosome and a deletion in another. Translocations can also rearrange material while leaving the total chromosome count unchanged. Some acquired translocations contribute to cancer by disrupting regulation or creating abnormal fusion genes. These examples show why counting chromosomes and examining their organisation answer different questions.

diagram.caption: A simplified unequal-exchange outcome: one product has an extra C segment while the other lacks C. Segment lengths and breakpoints are schematic.

slides.title: Use karyotypes for appropriate questions
slides.html: A karyotype can identify extra or missing chromosomes and sufficiently large rearrangements, but it cannot reveal every small DNA change. Its interpretation should specify the observed chromosome constitution and distinguish observation from predicted phenotype. A chromosome count cannot, by itself, establish the exact developmental outcome, the mechanism of origin or whether a rearrangement was inherited.

questions.prompt: Which description is aneuploidy rather than polyploidy?
options: Three complete sets of chromosomes
Four complete sets of chromosomes
One extra copy of a particular chromosome
An additional complete haploid set
feedback: Three complete sets is triploidy, a polyploid condition.
Four complete sets is tetraploidy, a polyploid condition.
Correct. Aneuploidy affects particular chromosome numbers rather than whole sets.
Adding a complete set changes ploidy, not simply one chromosome count.
questions.explanation: Correct. Aneuploidy affects particular chromosome numbers rather than whole sets.

questions.prompt: One homologous chromosome pair fails to separate in meiosis I. Meiosis II is otherwise normal. What products are expected?
options: Two n+1 and two n−1 gametes for the affected chromosome
Four normal gametes
Two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n−1
One triploid gamete and three diploid gametes
feedback: Correct. Both homologues entered one daughter cell, so all four products are affected for that pair.
The failure of homologues to separate changes the chromosome distribution.
This is the standard simplified outcome of one meiosis-II event after normal meiosis I.
The model concerns one pair, not gain of complete chromosome sets.
questions.explanation: Correct. Both homologues entered one daughter cell, so all four products are affected for that pair.

questions.prompt: A human gamete with 24 chromosomes fuses with a normal gamete containing 23. How many chromosomes does the resulting zygote contain?
questions.hint: Add the chromosome contributions of the two gametes.
questions.explanation: 24 + 23 = 47 chromosomes. Which chromosome is extra must be determined separately.

questions.prompt: Which observation is most consistent with mitotic nondisjunction after fertilisation?
options: Every gamete in a meiosis has exactly the same chromosome count.
A gene has a synonymous base substitution.
A protein contains one changed amino acid.
Different cell lineages in one individual have different chromosome numbers.
feedback: This describes meiotic products and does not establish a mitotic event.
A synonymous substitution does not imply different chromosome counts.
An amino-acid replacement is not evidence of chromosome-number mosaicism.
Correct. A post-zygotic mitotic error can produce mosaic cell populations.
questions.explanation: Correct. A post-zygotic mitotic error can produce mosaic cell populations.

questions.prompt: Compare the gamete outcomes of one nondisjunction event in meiosis I with one in meiosis II after a normal meiosis I.
questions.model: In meiosis I nondisjunction, both homologues enter one daughter cell. With otherwise normal meiosis II, all four gametes are affected for that pair: two have an extra copy and two lack a copy. If sister chromatids fail to separate in only one cell in meiosis II, the other cell can form normal products, giving two normal gametes, one n+1 and one n−1.
criteria: Identify homologues versus sister chromatids.
Give the four-product pattern for meiosis I.
Give the four-product pattern for meiosis II.

questions.prompt: Explain why a karyotype with 46 chromosomes is not proof that every chromosome has a typical structure or that the person has no genetic condition.
questions.model: A count of 46 specifies the total chromosome number, not the order and amount of every DNA region. A balanced rearrangement can retain 46 chromosomes while relocating or reversing material, and small substitutions or indels are below ordinary karyotype resolution. Gene expression and phenotype also require additional evidence. The karyotype should therefore be used for the scale of genetic change it can actually detect.
criteria: Separate chromosome count from structure.
Recognise small changes below karyotype resolution.
Avoid equating a count with a complete health prediction.

summary: Aneuploidy changes particular chromosomes; polyploidy changes complete sets.
Meiosis-I and meiosis-II nondisjunction produce different simplified gamete patterns.
Post-zygotic mitotic errors can create mosaic cell populations.
Chromosome count alone does not establish structure, origin or phenotype.

title: Gene Expression Affects Phenotype
objectives: Explain how cells with similar inherited DNA can differ in structure and function.
Relate promoters and regulation to functional gene products.
Distinguish a change in expression from a DNA-sequence mutation.

glossary.definition: Use of information in a gene to produce a functional RNA or polypeptide product.
A DNA region associated with transcription initiation where the transcription machinery assembles.
Development of specialised cell structures and functions.
Control of when, where and how much a gene product is produced.

slides.title: Having a gene is not the same as expressing it
slides.html: Most nucleated cells in a person inherit broadly the same genome, but they do not produce identical sets or amounts of gene products. Gene expression uses genetic information to make functional RNA or, for protein-coding genes, polypeptides. Which genes are active, and at what level, contributes to a cell’s structure, chemical reactions and responses.

slides.title: Shared genome, different cell roles
slides.html: A neuron and a skin epithelial cell need some shared products, such as those involved in basic metabolism, while requiring different specialised products. Regulatory networks establish and maintain these expression differences during differentiation. A cell does not normally become specialised by deleting every gene it does not use; the relevant information can remain while its activity differs.

diagram.caption: Matching segment labels illustrate shared inherited DNA, not identical expression. Different regulatory states can produce different cell functions without deleting the unused genes.

slides.title: Transcription is an important control point
slides.html: For a protein-coding gene, transcription begins when appropriate transcription machinery assembles at the promoter and related regulatory inputs permit initiation. In human cells this involves RNA polymerase and regulatory proteins. An altered promoter or a changed regulatory signal can reduce or increase transcription, even when the protein-coding sequence itself remains intact.

diagram.caption: This model highlights transcriptional control. RNA stability, translation and protein turnover are additional control points.

slides.title: Expression is more than a binary switch
slides.html: “On” and “off” are useful shorthand, but many genes are expressed at different levels rather than simply in two states. A cell can change the amount of a transcript, how an RNA is processed or how quickly a product is broken down. Consequently, a measurable expression difference need not mean that a new mutation has occurred.

slides.title: Proteins help produce a phenotype
slides.html: Structural proteins contribute to a cell’s physical organisation, while enzymes alter reaction rates and receptors influence responses to signals. Changing the amount or timing of one of these products can affect function. For example, producing less of an enzyme can limit a reaction even when the enzyme’s amino-acid sequence is unchanged. Product amount and product structure are different mechanisms.

slides.title: Environment and development influence expression
slides.html: Hormones, nutrients, developmental signals and other conditions can influence regulatory pathways. Some expression states are maintained through cell divisions by mechanisms that do not alter the underlying DNA sequence. Such regulation is not equivalent to every exposure changing inherited alleles. A phenotype can change within a lifetime without a corresponding change in the population’s allele frequencies.

slides.title: Misregulation and cancer biology
slides.html: Cell division is controlled by interacting regulatory pathways. Genes such as MYC participate in networks affecting growth and proliferation; inappropriate activity can contribute to cancer in particular contexts. Cancer is not simply every instance of rapid division, and no single expression change explains all tumours. Experiments that control a gene in engineered cells or animals test mechanisms, not automatic treatments for every human cancer.

slides.title: Interpret expression evidence cautiously
slides.html: If a group of genes is more active in one disease state than another, the association may help identify a biological pathway or a useful marker. It does not alone show whether the expression change caused the disease, resulted from it or reflects another influence. Controlled experiments, appropriate comparisons and replication are needed to distinguish these possibilities before making clinical claims.

questions.prompt: A neuron and an epithelial cell contain the same inherited gene but make different amounts of its protein. Which explanation best fits?
options: The gene must be absent from one cell.
The cells can regulate the gene differently.
Every difference in protein amount is a new mutation.
Both cells must perform identical functions.
feedback: Presence of the same gene does not imply identical expression.
Correct. Different regulatory states can produce different amounts of a product from shared DNA.
Expression changes can occur without a new DNA-sequence change.
Differences in expression help support specialised functions.
questions.explanation: Correct. Different regulatory states can produce different amounts of a product from shared DNA.

questions.prompt: What is a promoter’s role in the simplified transcription model?
options: It is the amino-acid chain produced by translation.
It is a whole extra chromosome.
It is a DNA region associated with assembly and initiation of transcription machinery.
It is always the same structure as a ribosome.
feedback: A promoter is DNA, not the translated polypeptide.
A promoter is a regulatory region, not a chromosome-number change.
Correct. Transcription initiation depends on appropriate machinery and regulatory input.
Ribosomes translate RNA and are not promoter DNA.
questions.explanation: Correct. Transcription initiation depends on appropriate machinery and regulatory input.

questions.prompt: Which observation necessarily demonstrates a new DNA-sequence mutation?
options: A transcript becomes more abundant after a hormonal signal.
A cell produces a different amount of an existing enzyme.
A gene is less active during differentiation.
Sequencing shows a base replacement relative to the original sequence.
feedback: Regulatory signalling can alter abundance without a new sequence change.
Protein amount can change through regulation or turnover.
Differentiation commonly involves expression changes rather than new mutations.
Correct. A demonstrated base replacement is direct sequence-change evidence.
questions.explanation: Correct. A demonstrated base replacement is direct sequence-change evidence.

questions.prompt: A gene-expression study finds that a transcript is more abundant in diseased tissue. What can be concluded from this observation alone?
options: The transcript abundance is associated with the sampled disease state.
The transcript has been proved to cause the disease.
Switching off that gene must cure every affected person.
All genes in the tissue have changed sequence.
feedback: Correct. Association is supported; causal direction and broader applicability require more evidence.
Association alone does not distinguish cause from consequence or confounding.
A universal treatment effect cannot be inferred from this association.
Expression abundance is not a genome-wide sequence-change measurement.
questions.explanation: Correct. Association is supported; causal direction and broader applicability require more evidence.

questions.prompt: Explain how two specialised cells can contain similar inherited DNA but differ in phenotype.
questions.model: Different cell types regulate which genes are expressed and the amounts, timing and processing of their products. A neuron and an epithelial cell can therefore make different specialised proteins while retaining broadly similar inherited genetic information. These products contribute to distinct structures and reactions. Their different phenotypes do not require deletion of all unused genes, and some shared housekeeping functions remain necessary in both cells.
criteria: Explain differential regulation with similar DNA.
Link gene products to specialised structure or function.
Reject deletion of all unused genes.

questions.prompt: A promoter change reduces production of an enzyme, but the enzyme molecules that are made have the original amino-acid sequence. Explain the possible effect and the evidence needed.
questions.model: Reduced transcription can lower the amount of enzyme produced without changing the coding sequence or the amino-acid sequence of each molecule. If enzyme availability limits the reaction, the relevant reaction rate and downstream products may change. Measurements of RNA, enzyme abundance and reaction activity would help test this mechanism. Other regulatory steps or compensating pathways must be considered rather than assuming reduced RNA alone proves the final phenotype.
criteria: Distinguish product amount from product sequence.
Link reduced expression to a possible functional consequence.
Identify measurements and a relevant limitation.

summary: Gene presence and gene expression are different.
Differential expression supports specialised cell phenotypes.
Regulation can change RNA or protein amounts without changing the coding sequence.
Expression associations do not alone establish causation or a clinical treatment.
sourceNotes: Scope follows Chapter 8, printed page 12.
Broadened gene expression to include functional RNA products and multiple control points.
The source’s engineered MYC/doxycycline example is not presented as a general antibiotic treatment for human cancer.
Promoter function and expression evidence are taught with regulatory and causal qualifications.

title: Allele Frequency
objectives: Calculate allele frequencies from genotype counts.
Distinguish a genome, gene pool and population.
State Hardy–Weinberg assumptions and predictions.

glossary.definition: The proportion of all allele copies at a defined locus represented by one allele.
All alleles present in a reproducing population.
A model in which allele and genotype frequencies remain constant under specified conditions.

slides.title: Define the population first
slides.html: A population is a group whose members reproduce with one another within a defined setting. A study must specify its boundaries, sampling time and locus. Two samples from different places need not represent the same breeding population. Frequencies describe that defined population, rather than every person carrying the same species name.

slides.title: Count allele copies, not visible traits
slides.html: At an autosomal locus in a diploid population, each person normally contributes two allele copies. An AA person contributes two A copies; an Aa person contributes one A and one a. Dominance affects the phenotype but does not change this accounting. A recessive allele can be common without being visibly expressed in most people.

diagram.caption: Each row represents a diploid genotype at one locus, not a whole chromosome. Count both copies.

slides.title: A worked frequency calculation
slides.html: Suppose 100 people include 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa individuals. There are 200 allele copies. A contributes 72 + 48 = 120 copies, so its frequency is 120/200 = 0.60. The a frequency is 0.40. These calculations use observed counts and do not require Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

slides.title: Genotype frequency is a different measure
slides.html: In the same example, the genotype frequencies are 0.36 AA, 0.48 Aa and 0.16 aa. Each denominator is 100 people, rather than 200 allele copies. If A is completely dominant, the A-associated phenotype frequency is 0.84, because AA and Aa contribute. That phenotype frequency is not the A allele frequency.

slides.title: Genomes and gene pools
slides.html: A genome is the complete genetic material of an organism, including coding and non-coding DNA. A gene pool is a population-level collection of alleles. Genomics compares or analyses genomes. The terms therefore refer to different scales: a person has a genome, while a defined reproducing population has a gene pool.

slides.title: The Hardy–Weinberg reference model
slides.html: For a two-allele autosomal locus, write p for the A frequency and q for the a frequency. Then p + q = 1. With random union of gametes, expected genotype frequencies are p² for AA, 2pq for Aa and q² for aa. The two heterozygote combinations explain the factor of two.

diagram.caption: Expected values under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model; this is not evidence that every population meets the assumptions.

slides.title: Conditions for equilibrium
slides.html: The model assumes a very large population, random mating with respect to the locus, no migration, no mutation and no natural selection at that locus. Large population size minimises random sampling effects. Real populations may approximate some conditions while violating others. Non-random mating alone can change genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele frequencies.

slides.title: Using the model carefully
slides.html: If the observed recessive phenotype frequency is 0.09 and aa alone produces it, equilibrium gives q² = 0.09, q = 0.30 and p = 0.70. Expected heterozygotes are 2pq = 0.42. Inferring carrier frequency this way requires the inheritance and equilibrium assumptions; phenotype counts alone do not establish them.

questions.prompt: A sample contains 20 AA, 50 Aa and 30 aa people. What is the A allele frequency?
questions.hint: Count two A copies for AA and one for Aa, then divide by twice the number of people.
questions.explanation: A copies = 2 × 20 + 50 = 90. Total copies = 200. Frequency = 90/200 = 0.45.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is an allele frequency?
options: People with a dominant phenotype divided by people sampled
A copies divided by all copies at that locus
AA people divided by people sampled
All genes divided by chromosomes
feedback: A dominant phenotype can include two genotypes, so this is a phenotype frequency.
Correct: allele frequency counts copies at a locus.
This is an AA genotype frequency.
Genes and chromosomes are not the alternative allele copies being counted.
questions.explanation: Correct: allele frequency counts copies at a locus.

questions.prompt: Under Hardy–Weinberg assumptions, q = 0.20. What is the expected heterozygote frequency?
questions.hint: First calculate p = 1 − q, then use 2pq.

questions.prompt: Which condition belongs to the Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium model?
options: Only dominant alleles reproduce
Individuals choose mates with the same genotype
No natural selection at the locus
Every person has an identical genome
feedback: Dominance does not decide which alleles enter gametes.
Genotype-based mating violates random mating at that locus.
Correct: differential reproductive success would disturb the model.
Genetic variation can persist at equilibrium.
questions.explanation: Correct: differential reproductive success would disturb the model.

questions.prompt: Explain why a dominant phenotype frequency cannot normally be used directly as the dominant allele frequency.
questions.model: An allele frequency counts allele copies, whereas a phenotype frequency counts individuals showing a trait. With complete dominance, both AA and Aa individuals show the dominant phenotype. They contribute different numbers of A copies: two and one respectively. A phenotype count therefore does not separate these contributions. Genotype information, or additional justified assumptions, is needed to infer the allele frequency.
criteria: Distinguishes allele copies from individuals
Explains that AA and Aa share the phenotype
States their different A-copy contributions

questions.prompt: A class estimates carrier frequency from a recessive phenotype count. Explain two assumptions it must justify.
questions.model: The class must establish that the phenotype follows the proposed autosomal recessive model, so the affected group can represent aa rather than a mixture of causes. It must also justify approximating Hardy–Weinberg conditions for the sampled locus and population. Only then can it identify the affected frequency as q², calculate q and estimate carriers with 2pq. A representative sample is also needed.
criteria: Links the phenotype to aa
Identifies equilibrium assumptions
Explains the q² to 2pq reasoning

summary: Allele frequency counts copies at a locus.
Observed genotype counts permit direct allele counting.
Hardy–Weinberg predictions require explicit assumptions.
